doc_description: SEC Form 10-K of PayPal Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: PYPL) for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022—an audited annual report by PwC covering the company’s one-segment global digital payments platforms (PayPal, Venmo, Braintree, Xoom, Zettle, Honey, Paidy), 2022 results ($27.5B revenue; $1.36T TPV), extensive risk and regulatory disclosures, MD&A, BNPL and merchant credit portfolios, adoption of crypto safeguarding accounting (SAB 121), share repurchases (new $15B authorization) and $10.4B debt, with Part III information incorporated by reference to the 2023 proxy.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K cover for PayPal Holdings, Inc. for fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, filed under Sections 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act.
- Company identification and listing details: Delaware corporation, EIN 47-2989869, principal office in San Jose, CA; NASDAQ ticker PYPL; common stock registered under Section 12(b); no Section 12(g) securities.
- Compliance and filer status: well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; timely filing of reports and interactive data; auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting under SOX 404(b); not a shell company.
- Market and capital structure data: aggregate market value of non-affiliate common stock as of June 30, 2022 (~$80.7B); shares outstanding as of Feb 3, 2023 (1,131,373,298).
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2023 definitive proxy statement into Part III.
- Table of Contents outlining Parts I–IV, including Business, Risk Factors, MD&A, Market Risk, Financial Statements, Controls and Procedures, and other standard 10-K items.
- Trademarks and brands: references to key brands and platforms such as PayPal, PayPal Credit, Braintree, Venmo, Xoom, Zettle, Hyperwallet, Honey, and Paidy, with notice on usage and rights.
- Forward-looking statements safe harbor: identification of forward-looking terms and caution regarding risks and uncertainties, with reference to Risk Factors (Item 1A) and other SEC filings.
- Item 1—Business (overview excerpt): PayPal as a leading global technology platform enabling digital payments and commerce for merchants and consumers, including P2P; mission to democratize financial services; focus on enabling money movement globally across platforms and devices; emphasis on core values (Inclusion, Innovation, Collaboration, Wellness) and ESG considerations; clarification that references to “PayPal” include PayPal Holdings, Inc. and consolidated subsidiaries.

- Business overview of PayPal: Incorporated in Delaware in 2015, PayPal is a leading global technology platform for digital payments, serving merchants and consumers with solutions that enable money movement and commerce, including P2P payments, across devices and platforms.
- Mission and strategy: Committed to democratizing financial services to improve financial health and expand economic opportunity for individuals and businesses of all sizes worldwide.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: PayPal Holdings, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware in January 2015 and is a leading technology platform that enables digital payments and simplifies commerce experiences on behalf of merchants and consumers worldwide.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements caution, referencing risks, uncertainties, and no obligation to update.
- Item 1. Business: PayPal overview, mission to democratize financial services, two-sided global payments platform across 200+ markets with 435M active accounts (400M consumers, 35M merchants) and $1.36T TPV in 2022; brands include PayPal, Braintree, Venmo, Xoom, Hyperwallet, Zettle, Honey, Paidy.
- Revenue model: transaction fees, FX conversion, instant transfer and crypto fees, interest and fees from consumer and merchant credit, interest on certain customer balance assets, partnerships, referrals, subscriptions, and gateway services.
- Key metrics defined: Total Payment Volume, number of payment transactions, and active accounts.
- Competitive strengths: two-sided network, merchant/consumer choice across funding methods, global scale, trusted brands, risk & compliance capabilities, and regulatory licenses.
- Merchant solutions: full-stack online and in-store checkout (branded and unbranded via Braintree), alternative payments, risk/fraud tools, analytics, returns/exchanges support, PayPal Zettle POS, and merchant financing (PayPal Working Capital and Business Loan); merchant revenues from fees and credit interest/fees.
- Consumer solutions: digital wallets (PayPal, Venmo) with multiple funding sources, P2P (PayPal, Venmo, Xoom), shopping tools and rewards, BNPL and other credit products across the U.S., U.K., EU, Japan (via Paidy), and Germany; crypto buy/hold/sell/send/receive in certain markets; consumer revenues from fees (FX, instant transfer, crypto), and credit interest/fees.
- Protections: buyer and seller protection programs and robust fraud prevention leveraging two-sided data and proprietary risk systems.
- Competition: intense global competition from banks, networks, processors, wallets, BNPL, RTP systems, P2P/remittance providers, POS devices, and crypto; differentiation via innovation, ease of use, protections, analytics, and omnichannel reach.
- Strategy: grow core business and engagement, expand merchant and consumer value propositions, deepen strategic partnerships, and pursue organic/inorganic growth and innovation.
- ESG management: enterprise-wide approach across employees/culture, social innovation, environmental sustainability, and responsible business practices; climate initiatives, financial inclusion investments, inclusion and safety focus; annual Global Impact Report.
- Technology: scalable, resilient, multi-currency platform (send in nearly 150 currencies, withdraw in 56, hold in 25), APIs/developer tools, hybrid data center/cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity program and resiliency best practices.
- R&D expense: $1.7B (2022), $1.6B (2021), $1.4B (2020).
- Intellectual property: trademarks, domains, copyrights, patents, trade secrets, and contractual protections; notes related IP risk factors.
- Government regulation: extensive global payments, banking, lending, consumer protection, privacy/data protection, AML/CFT/sanctions, interchange, and anti-corruption oversight.
  - U.S. money transmitter licenses (including for Venmo, Hyperwallet, Xoom) and a NY BitLicense; EU/U.K./APAC oversight (e.g., CSSF, FCA); PayPal (Europe) regulated as a Luxembourg credit institution; authentication/Strong Customer Authentication requirements.
  - Lending regulations for BNPL and installment products vary by market; some products issued by partner banks.
  - CFPB supervision (including remittances); AML/sanctions programs; evolving privacy/data protection regimes; ESG-related disclosure rules.
- Human capital: ~29,900 employees across 27 countries; engagement survey results (79% engagement, 78% intent to stay); leadership principles; talent acquisition/development, coaching and mentorship; wellness benefits; DIE&B commitment with representation metrics, pay equity focus, ERGs; flexible/hybrid workplace; additional metrics in Global Impact Report.
- Available information: corporate and investor relations websites, SEC filings access, and use of designated social channels for disclosures (with non-incorporation notice).
- Item 1A. Risk Factors (beginning): cybersecurity and technology risks, including evolving cyber threats, data breaches (with TIO example), third-party/vendor risks, potential liabilities, operational and reputational impacts, and limits of insurance; mention of business interruptions/system failures risk.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
You should carefully consider the risks and uncertainties described below, in addition to other information appearing in this Form 10-K, including our
consolidated financial statements and related notes, for important information regarding risks and uncertainties that could affect us.
structure.summary:
- The document is a 10-K Risk Factors section outlining material risks that could adversely affect the company’s business, financial condition, results, and stock price, followed by brief disclosures on unresolved staff comments and properties.

- Cybersecurity and technology risks:
  - Increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, data breaches, fraud, ransomware, DDoS, insider threats, and vulnerabilities across company, vendors, partners, customers, and acquired entities.
  - Potential for regulatory investigations, fines, litigation, reputational harm, customer loss, operational disruption, and insufficient insurance coverage.
  - Business interruptions from natural disasters, power/telecom failures, pandemics, climate-related events, hardware/software failures; disaster recovery and resiliency requirements and costs.
  - Risks from system upgrades/re-platforming, reliance on third-party data centers/cloud providers, and failure to implement new technologies.
  - Risk of not keeping pace with rapid technological change (real-time payments, tokenization, crypto/blockchain, AI/ML, browser and commerce tech), third-party/platform constraints, and regulatory uncertainty.

- Legal, regulatory, and compliance risks:
  - Extensive, evolving global regulation of payments, money transmission, banking, data, privacy, AML/CTF, sanctions, consumer protection, competition, and crypto.
  - U.S. money transmitter licensing compliance risks; limits in certain markets on receiving payments.
  - EU/EEA and U.K.: PayPal (Europe) regulated as a Luxembourg credit institution; potential ECB supervision and PISA obligations; costs/complexity and inconsistent interpretations.
  - Singapore: licensing under the Payment Services Act; new requirements may add complexity and costs; uncertainty over extra-territorial application of local laws in other markets.
  - Cryptocurrency: unclear asset classifications; potential SEC and other regulatory obligations; custodial, operational, cybersecurity, insurance, and bankruptcy risks regarding third-party crypto custody.
  - Lending: U.S. state lending licenses; global scrutiny of short-term installment/BNPL; possible product and compliance changes and enforcement exposure.
  - Consumer protection: EFTA/Reg E litigation and CFPB information orders; possibility of broader EU/U.K. consumer law application via passporting/temporary permissions.
  - AML/CTF and sanctions: rising standards, more friction and costs, potential penalties and restrictions for non-compliance.
  - Privacy/data protection: evolving laws (EU SCCs, Binding Corporate Rules, proliferating U.S. state laws); cross-border data transfer constraints and added obligations; enforcement, fines, and operational impacts.
  - Antitrust/competition scrutiny: potential investigations, private actions, remedial measures, and delayed transactions.
  - Ongoing litigation and regulatory matters: uncertainty, costs, reputational harm, potential for material judgments or settlements.
  - IP risks: third-party infringement claims and challenges protecting/enforcing proprietary rights globally.

- Business and operations risks:
  - Intense global competition from established and emerging players; partner relationship competition and dependence.
  - Payment network rules/fees and interchange regulation changes; risk of fines or required business practice changes.
  - Adverse shifts in consumer funding mix toward higher-cost payment cards.
  - U.S. bank partnership model risks (valid-when-made doctrine uncertainty); potential impact on merchant financing and certain installment products.
  - Credit product risks: underwriting/model performance, economic conditions, defaults, partner bank dependence, funding capacity.
  - Third-party reliance: processors, banks, issuers, custodians, outsourcers; migration risks from primary processor change; diminished control and added compliance/operational risk.
  - Cross-border trade exposure to FX, tariffs, sanctions, trade barriers, and multi-jurisdictional legal complexity.
  - Fraud, abusive behaviors, chargebacks, and losses under buyer/seller protection programs; potential loss of card acceptance.
  - Illegal or improper platform use (e.g., money laundering, sanctions evasion, illicit goods/services) leading to enforcement, restrictions, and reputational harm.
  - Strategic transactions (M&A, investments, partnerships) integration and regulatory risks, potential impairments, dilution, and diverted management attention.
  - International operations complexities: localization, staffing, compliance, FX, repatriation, trade restrictions, anti-bribery/corruption exposure, and geopolitical instability.
  - Macroeconomic volatility: financial market stress, inflation/deflation, unemployment, consumer confidence, supply chain, liquidity access, and FX/interest rate impacts.
  - Brand/reputation risks amplified by social media and policy/product decisions.
  - Brexit-related regulatory divergence, permissions, and cost/complexity; risks to U.K. market access under the Temporary Permissions Regime.
  - Key metrics accuracy and methodology changes; potential investor skepticism and reputational effects.
  - ESG and climate risks: stakeholder expectations, regulatory reporting, operational disruptions (e.g., California climate events), and increased costs.
  - Counterparty financial institution failures or defaults affecting deposits, derivatives, credit facilities, and access to assets.
  - Indebtedness risks: servicing costs, covenant restrictions, potential accelerations, ratings impacts, and financing access.
  - Tax risks: changing laws (including digital services taxes), audits, uncertain outcomes, reserve adequacy, and marketplace reporting/record-keeping obligations.
  - Talent risks: competition for skilled workers, immigration/visa constraints, retention and culture challenges.
  - Liability for information disseminated via services if protections are reduced; potential need for costly controls or product changes.

- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: None.

- Item 2. Properties: Summary of owned and leased global facilities totaling approximately 5.3 million square feet (about 3.2 million in the U.S., 2.1 million in other countries), roughly 106 acres of land (about 85 acres in the U.S.), with corporate headquarters in San Jose, California occupying approximately 0.7 million owned square feet.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
This Form 10-K contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 21E of the Securities
Exchange Act of 1934, including statements that involve expectations, plans, or intentions (such as those relating to future business, future results of operations
or financial condition, new or planned features or services, mergers or acquisitions, or management strategies).
structure.summary:
- Scope and framing: Management’s Discussion and Analysis focuses on 2022 vs. 2021 performance, includes a forward‑looking statements caution, and directs readers to prior filings for 2021 vs. 2020 comparisons.

- Business overview and environment:
  - Company: PayPal is a global digital payments and commerce enablement platform serving merchants and consumers.
  - Regulatory landscape: Heightened global focus on AML, sanctions, privacy, cybersecurity, and consumer protection; evolving laws and enforcement could materially affect results.
  - Information security: Elevated cyber risk despite ongoing investments; potential for breaches remains.
  - Russia–Ukraine: Services in Russia suspended in March 2022; revenue exposure to Russia/Ukraine not material.
  - Brexit: Operating in the U.K. under the Temporary Permissions Regime while seeking new authorizations; potential FX and regulatory impacts; shares of revenue and loan exposure in U.K./EU provided.
  - Macroeconomy: Uncertainty from COVID-19 aftereffects, war, supply chains, inflation, rising rates, and potential recession could pressure spending, credit losses, FX, and operating results.

- Consolidated results (2022 vs. 2021 with 2020 context):
  - Net revenues up 8% to $27.5B, driven by 9% TPV growth.
  - Operating expenses up 12% to $23.7B (higher transaction expense, transaction/credit losses, tech & development, restructuring; lower sales & marketing).
  - Operating income down 10% to $3.8B; margin fell to 14% from 17%.
  - Net income down 42% to $2.4B due to lower operating income, higher other expense (strategic investment losses), and higher income tax expense.
  - Cash from operations steady at $5.8B.
  - FX: 2022 saw an unfavorable revenue impact partly offset by hedging; minimal net impact on operating income.

- Key operating metrics and revenue drivers:
  - Definitions provided for TPV, payment transactions, active accounts, and transactions per active account.
  - 2022 metrics: 435M active accounts (+2%), 22.3B transactions (+16%), TPV $1.36T (+9%), 51.4 transactions per active account (+13%); cross‑border TPV fell to 13%.
  - Transaction revenues +8%: strength in unbranded card processing (Braintree) and Venmo; offset by declines in core PayPal (including eBay marketplace volumes and FX fees). Included $190M in contractual compensation from sellers violating terms (mostly international).
  - Other value‑added services +17%: higher interest on customer balance assets (rising rates), partner revenue share, merchant loan interest/fees; prior‑year PPP servicing fees rolled off. Revenue share from branded credit subject to minimum return thresholds.

- Operating expenses detail:
  - Transaction expense +18% (higher TPV, mix shift to higher‑cost unbranded card processing); expense rate increased to 0.90%.
  - Transaction and credit losses +48%: transaction losses ~flat at ~$1.2B (Venmo fraud schemes, broader protection coverage, one merchant insolvency offset by recoveries); credit losses moved to expense due to reserve build and higher net charge‑offs with loan growth.
  - Credit portfolios:
    - Consumer loans net receivable up 53% to $5.9B (installment growth; U.K. share declined as other markets grew). Credit quality remained strong (97% current; net charge‑off rate ~4.5%).
    - Merchant receivables up 48% to $2.1B (U.S. growth); slight credit quality softening but stable net charge‑off rate ~4.5%.
  - Customer support & operations +2%; Sales & marketing −8% (lower campaigns); Technology & development +7% (people, cloud); G&A −1%.
  - Restructuring and other charges increased (workforce reduction to streamline operations; real estate impairments related to space exits).

- Other income (expense) and taxes:
  - Other income (expense), net worsened due to strategic investment losses and higher interest expense, partially offset by higher interest income.
  - Effective tax rate rose to 28% from −2%, driven by lower stock‑based comp tax benefits and IP transfer taxes.

- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Cash, cash equivalents, and investments: $13.7B (62% held by foreign subs; subject to regulatory needs and global cash management).
  - 2022 cash flows: Operating $5.8B; Investing $(3.4)B (loan originations, securities purchases; offset by repayments/maturities); Financing $(1.1)B (share repurchases, debt repayments; offset by new debt and higher customer liabilities).
  - Credit facilities and debt: $5.0B undrawn revolver; Paidy ¥90B facility (portion drawn); $10.4B fixed‑rate notes outstanding after 2022 issuance and partial redemptions; investment‑grade ratings maintained.
  - Cash pooling arrangement utilized for liquidity optimization.

- Current and future cash needs:
  - Uses include operations, customer protection, credit funding, capex, M&A/strategic investments, repurchases.
  - Credit products funding: CSSF authorization to designate a portion of European customer balances (up to ~50% through Feb 2023; $3.8B designated cumulatively) to fund credit; seeking more external funding sources.
  - Customer protection loss rates historically 0.09%–0.12% of TPV but subject to change.
  - Share repurchases: $4.2B in 2022; remaining authorizations ~$0.9B (2018 program) and $15.0B (new 2022 program).
  - Future obligations detailed for purchase commitments, leases, transition tax, and long‑term debt; additional uncertain tax positions not scheduled.

- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Allowances for transaction and credit losses (CECL modeling, macroeconomic overlays; sensitivity noted).
  - Income tax accounting (rate drivers, deferred tax realizability, uncertain tax positions; sensitivity to rate changes).
  - Loss contingencies (legal/regulatory matters).
  - Revenue recognition judgments (principal vs. agent, incentives).
  - Valuation of goodwill/intangibles and impairment assessments.
  - Valuation and impairment of non‑marketable strategic investments.

- Market risk management:
  - Quantitative and qualitative disclosures on interest rate, foreign exchange, and equity investment risks; use of hedging (cash flow, net investment, and balance sheet hedges) and daily FX rate setting on platform.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: Market risk is the potential for economic losses to be incurred on market risk sensitive instruments arising from adverse changes in market factors such as interest rates, foreign currency exchange rates, and equity investment risk.
structure.summary:
- Loss contingencies: Ongoing claims, regulatory/legal proceedings, and investigations are evaluated regularly; liabilities are accrued when losses are probable and reasonably estimable. Significant judgment is involved, estimates are reassessed as new information emerges, and actual outcomes may differ materially.
- Revenue recognition: Complex contracts require judgment under U.S. GAAP, including principal vs. agent determinations. Consumer/merchant incentives may reduce revenue if considered customer consideration. Changes in assumptions can affect recognized revenue.
- Valuation of goodwill and intangibles: Business combinations require fair value estimates to allocate purchase price among assets, liabilities, NCI, and goodwill. Estimates rely on management assumptions and are inherently uncertain.
- Strategic investments impairment: Non-marketable equity securities are measured under the Measurement Alternative (cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes). Impairment is assessed using qualitative factors; when indicated, fair value is estimated (market/income approaches) and write-downs flow through other income (expense).
- Market risk (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate risk: Cash/investment portfolio held largely in cash/cash equivalents (57% in 2022; 40% in 2021), with the remainder in deposits and AFS debt; assets maintained to cover 100% of customer balances. A 100 bps increase would reduce fair value of cash equivalents/AFS debt by ~$161M (2022) and ~$272M (2021). Fixed-rate debt of $10.4B (2022) and $9.0B (2021) has fair value sensitivity but no interest expense risk; revolving credit facilities of ~$5.7B (2022) and ~$5.2B (2021) bear floating rates with ¥64.3B (~$491M) and ¥11.3B (~$98M) drawn, respectively; a 100 bps increase would not be material to interest expense. Higher rates may increase customer delinquencies/charge-offs.
  - Foreign currency risk: Significant exposure to GBP, EUR, AUD, CAD; company is a net receiver of foreign currencies (benefits from weaker USD). A 10% exchange-rate move is considered reasonably possible. Hedging includes cash flow and net investment forward contracts (AOCI impacts), plus non-designated balance sheet hedges. A 10% USD weakening would lower AOCI related to forwards by ~$710M (2022) and ~$512M (2021). A 10% adverse move would impact income before taxes by ~$173M (2022) and ~$196M (2021) pre-hedge; hedges reduce the net impact to approximately -$29M (2022) and +$7M (2021).
  - Equity investment risk: Strategic investments totaled $2.1B (14% of portfolio) in 2022 and $3.2B (20%) in 2021, including marketable and non-marketable securities; all value adjustments flow through earnings, creating expected P&L volatility. A 10% adverse change would reduce carrying value by ~$215M. Liquidity of private holdings depends on future events; ongoing impairment reviews consider financial and market factors.

- Document scope: PayPal Holdings, Inc. consolidated Statements of Stockholders’ Equity and Cash Flows, presented in millions, covering years ended December 31, 2020–2022 (with 2019 opening balances for equity).

- Stockholders’ equity:
  - Key drivers each year include net income, other comprehensive income (loss) from foreign currency translation, cash flow and net investment hedges, unrealized gains/losses on investments with related tax effects, stock-based compensation, share issuances/net share settlements, and significant share repurchases.
  - Adoption of the current expected credit loss (CECL) standard in 2020 reduced retained earnings.
  - Consistent, large buybacks reduced common shares outstanding (from ~1,173M at 2019 year-end to ~1,136M by 2022) and increased treasury stock balance (more negative).
  - Additional paid-in capital rose primarily from stock-based compensation, partially offset by shares issued/withheld for taxes.
  - Accumulated other comprehensive income swung negative, particularly in 2022, driven by unrealized losses on investments and FX/hedge impacts.
  - Retained earnings increased each year with ongoing profitability.
  - Noncontrolling interest was eliminated by 2022.
  - Total equity trajectory: grew from 2019 through 2021, then declined in 2022 due to buybacks and OCI losses, ending around $20.3B.

- Cash flows:
  - Operating activities: strong, stable cash generation (~$5.8–$6.2B annually), with adjustments including transaction/credit losses, depreciation/amortization, stock-based compensation, deferred taxes, and fair value changes on strategic investments.
  - Investing activities: dominated by the loans receivable portfolio (originations vs. principal repayments) and investment securities (purchases vs. maturities/sales); included acquisitions in 2020–2021; overall net cash used improved from 2020 to 2022.
  - Financing activities: characterized by substantial share repurchases each year, issuances related to equity awards (with tax withholdings), periodic borrowings/repayments, and changes in customer funds payable; net financing cash inflows in 2020 turned to outflows in 2021–2022.
  - Liquidity: ending cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash increased to roughly $19.2B at 2022 year-end, with modest FX impacts reported each year.

nodes.title: Basis of presentation and principles of consolidation
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.1 Basis of presentation and principles of consolidation
nodes.start_phrase: The accompanying consolidated financial statements include the financial statements of PayPal and our wholly- and majority-owned subsidiaries.
nodes.summary:

Operates in a highly regulated environment with evolving laws on AML, counter-terrorist financing, privacy, cybersecurity, and consumer protection that could materially impact results.
- Basis of presentation and consolidation: Consolidated financial statements include wholly- and majority-owned subsidiaries with all intercompany items eliminated. Equity method applied where PayPal has significant influence; otherwise investments measured at fair value or cost minus impairment with adjustments for observable price changes, with results recorded in other income (expense), net.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.5 Investments
nodes.start_phrase: Short-term investments include time deposits and available-for-sale debt securities with original maturities of greater than three months but less than one year when purchased or maturities of one year or less on the reporting date.
nodes.summary:
- Restatement/reclassification of 2020 consolidated statements of cash flows: Operating cash flows increased by $365 million, investing decreased by $327 million, and financing decreased by $38 million, with no change to total net cash increase ($2,297 million) or FX effects; changes reported in the 2021 Form 10-K. Impacted lines included other current/non-current assets and liabilities (operating) and collateral posted/received related to derivative instruments (investing/financing).
- Summary of significant accounting policies and use of estimates: Management’s ongoing estimates affect credit and transaction loss provisions, income taxes, contingencies, revenue recognition, goodwill and intangible asset valuations, and strategic investment valuations; actual results may differ materially.
- Cash and cash equivalents policy: Highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less, including bank deposits, government/agency securities, and commercial paper.
- Investment accounting:
  - Classification of short-term and long-term investments; available-for-sale (AFS) debt securities measured at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in other comprehensive income (OCI).
  - Election of the fair value option for certain AFS debt securities denominated in non-functional currencies, funds receivable and customer accounts, and certain short- and long-term investments, with changes recognized in other income (expense), net.
  - Strategic investments include marketable equity securities (fair value through earnings) and non-marketable equity securities measured using the measurement alternative or the equity method; all related gains/losses and equity method results recognized in other income (expense), net.
- Impairment and credit loss methodology:
  - Non-marketable (measurement alternative) and equity method investments assessed for impairment using qualitative factors and fair value techniques; impairments recognized in other income (expense), net.
  - AFS debt securities written down through earnings if sale is intended or likely required before recovery; otherwise, credit losses recorded via an allowance (limited to fair value shortfall) with non-credit losses in OCI.
- Loans and interest receivable, net:
  - Portfolio includes PPWC and PPBL merchant receivables and consumer receivables from PayPal Credit and installment products, originated via a U.S. partner bank and various international subsidiaries.
  - In the U.S., PayPal purchases receivables originated by the partner institution; sells back pro rata participation interests to the partner, with shared credit risk and no recourse; transfers accounted for as sales with derecognition; gains/losses on transfers not material.

nodes.title: Loans and interest receivable, net
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.6 Loans and interest receivable, net
nodes.start_phrase: Loans and interest receivable, net represents merchant receivables originated under our PayPal Working Capital (“PPWC”) product and PayPal Business Loan (“PPBL”) product and consumer loans originated under our PayPal Credit and installment credit products.
nodes.summary:
- Describes accounting for strategic investments:
  - Marketable equity securities measured at fair value with changes in other income (expense), net.
  - Non-marketable equity securities accounted for under the measurement alternative (cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes) or the equity method when significant influence exists; all related gains/losses and equity method results recorded in other income (expense), net.
  - Impairment assessments for non-marketable and equity method investments based on qualitative factors; fair value estimated via market and/or income approaches; write-downs recorded in other income (expense), net.
  - Available-for-sale debt securities: write down to fair value through earnings if intent/requirement to sell exists; otherwise record allowance for credit losses for the credit component, with non-credit losses in other comprehensive income.

- Details on loans and interest receivable, net:
  - Portfolio includes merchant receivables (PPWC, PPBL) and consumer credit (PayPal Credit and installment products).
  - U.S. origination via a partner bank for merchant and interest-bearing consumer installment products; PayPal purchases receivables. International origination through Luxembourg banking subsidiary and local subsidiaries in Australia and Japan; certain U.S. short-term, interest-free installments issued by a U.S. subsidiary.
  - PayPal sells participation interests in U.S. PPWC, PPBL, and interest-bearing installment pools back to the partner bank; risks shared pro rata; transfers accounted for as sales with derecognition of sold interests; gains/losses immaterial.
  - Troubled debt restructurings may occur for financially distressed merchants.
  - PayPal services the entire pool and earns market-based servicing fees.
  - A separate partner bank exclusively issues U.S. PayPal Credit consumer financing; PayPal does not own these receivables and recognizes a revenue share in revenues from other value added services.

- Allowance for loans and interest receivable (CECL):
  - Estimates current expected credit losses; increases recorded in transaction and credit losses (for loans) or as reductions of net revenues/deferred revenue (for interest and fees).
  - CECL adopted effective January 1, 2020.
  - Merchant loss models use historical lifetime loss data, portfolio attributes (geography, first vs. repeat borrowing, delinquency, internal risk ratings, vintage), and externally sourced macroeconomic forecasts (e.g., unemployment, retail e-commerce trends; earlier included benchmark credit card charge-offs); reasonable and supportable forecast horizon ~2.5–3.5 years; includes qualitative adjustments.
  - Interest and fees receivable allowances determined using loss curves by geography, delinquency, and origination period.

nodes.title: Allowance for loans and interest receivable
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.7 Allowance for loans and interest receivable
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for loans and interest receivable represents our estimate of current expected credit losses inherent in our portfolio of loans and interest receivables.
nodes.summary:
- Explains when merchant loan or advance modifications constitute troubled debt restructurings (TDRs) and references Note 11 for details.
- Describes recognition of loans, advances, and interest/fee receivables at outstanding balances net of participation interests sold and deferred origination costs; PayPal retains servicing rights and earns a market-based servicing fee.
- Outlines consumer credit offerings (revolving and installment), monthly billing, ability to charge interest/fees, and that consumer balances are generally unsecured.
- Notes that a partner institution exclusively issues the U.S. PayPal Credit consumer program; PayPal does not record those receivables and recognizes a revenue share in “revenues from other value added services.”
- Details the allowance for loans and interest receivable under CECL (ASU 2016-13 adopted January 1, 2020), including estimation of current expected credit losses and where changes are recognized in the income statement.
- Merchant receivables allowance: based on historical lifetime losses, macroeconomic forecasts (e.g., unemployment, retail e-commerce sales; credit card charge-offs through Q2’22), portfolio attributes (geography, first vs. repeat borrowing, delinquency, internal risk ratings, vintage), single externally sourced scenario, 2.5–3.5 year reasonable and supportable forecast horizon, qualitative adjustments; 2022 model updates had no material impact; interest/fee allowance uses loss curves.
- Consumer receivables allowance: based on historical lifetime losses with macro forecasts for revolving products (unemployment, household disposable income); attributes include geography, term, delinquency, credit rating, vintage; forecast horizons of ~2 years (revolving) and ~7 months–3.5 years (installment) in 2022 (installment was ~7 months–2.5 years in 2021); qualitative overlays; interest/fee allowance uses loss curves.
- Clarifies treatment of customer balances: recorded as a liability (“amounts due to customers”); certain jurisdictions require eligible liquid assets equal to 100% of customer balances, classified as current “customer accounts”; some agent/custodian funds (e.g., U.S. dollar funds at FDIC-insured banks) are off-balance sheet with pass-through insurance eligibility.
- Addresses cryptocurrency custody: PayPal acts as agent; crypto held for customers is not a company asset; recognizes a safeguarding liability with a corresponding safeguarding asset.
- Describes CSSF approvals allowing designation of a portion of European customer balances in the Luxembourg banking subsidiary to fund credit activities (from 35% to 50% through Feb 2023); $1.1B additional approved in 2022, cumulative $3.8B (≈37%) designated at 12/31/22; designated amounts reclassified to cash and cash equivalents; remaining customer balances remain in “customer accounts” and are held in bank deposits, time deposits, and available-for-sale debt securities; certain short-term partner deposits are classified as cash and cash equivalents within customer accounts.
- States that changes in funds receivable and customer accounts are presented as investing cash flows.

nodes.title: Customer accounts
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.8 Customer accounts
nodes.start_phrase: We hold all customer balances, both in the U.S. and internationally, as direct claims against us which are reflected on our consolidated balance sheets as a liability classified as amounts due to customers.
nodes.summary:
- Credit loss methodology: Describes PayPal’s allowance for consumer loans and interest/fees receivable using lifetime expected credit loss models based on historical loss data, portfolio attributes, and for revolving credit, externally sourced macroeconomic forecasts (e.g., unemployment, household disposable income) under a single scenario. Includes qualitative adjustments for factors not captured in models. Forecast horizons: approx. 2 years for revolving products; 7 months–3.5 years for installment products in 2022 (previously 7 months–2.5 years in 2021).
- Measurement of interest/fees CECL: Loss curves applied by geography, delinquency, and origination period.
- Customer accounts and regulatory segregation: Customer balances are liabilities (“amounts due to customers”) with corresponding restricted assets classified as “customer accounts,” held as eligible liquid assets equal to at least 100% of balances in certain jurisdictions. These are current and segregated from corporate funds.
- Treatment of agent custodial funds: Customer funds held as agent (e.g., certain U.S. dollar deposits with FDIC pass-through eligibility) are not on the balance sheet.
- Cryptocurrency safeguarding: PayPal acts as agent for customer crypto; records a safeguarding asset and corresponding liability, but no crypto assets on its own balance sheet.
- Use of European customer balances for credit: CSSF approvals allow designation of up to 50% of Luxembourg-held European balances (through Feb 2023) to fund credit activities; $1.1B additional designated in 2022; cumulative $3.8B (about 37% of eligible balances) designated as of Dec 31, 2022. Designated balances reclassified to cash and cash equivalents; remaining segregated as customer accounts and invested in deposits, time deposits, and AFS debt securities.
- Cash flow presentation: Changes in funds receivable and customer accounts presented as investing cash flows.
- Funds receivable/payable: Arise from settlement clearing times with external networks—typically 1–3 business days in the U.S. and up to 5 days internationally; includes funds settled directly to customers’ bank accounts.
- Property and equipment: Stated at cost less depreciation; useful lives include 1–4 years for computer/software, 3 years for furniture, up to 30 years for buildings, and shorter of 5 years or lease term for leasehold improvements. Internal-use software and website development costs are capitalized (2022: $511M; 2021: $462M) and amortized (2022: $426M; 2021: $366M; 2020: $322M); maintenance expensed.
- Leases: Operating leases recognized as ROU assets and lease liabilities (measured using incremental borrowing rate), with straight-line expense. Sale-leaseback transactions evaluated for transfer of control; if financing method applies, asset remains on balance sheet and proceeds recorded as a financing obligation. ROU assets tested for impairment upon indicators, including decisions to exit or sublease, using undiscounted cash flows and fair value measurements at the appropriate asset group level.

nodes.title: Funds receivable and funds payable
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.9 Funds receivable and funds payable
nodes.start_phrase: Funds receivable and funds payable arise due to the time required to initiate collection from and clear transactions through external payment networks.
nodes.summary:
- Explains “funds receivable and funds payable” arising from clearing times in external payment networks, typically 1–3 business days for U.S. and up to 5 for international transactions, including amounts settled directly to customers’ bank accounts.
- Details property and equipment components (computer equipment, software and website development, land/buildings, leasehold improvements, furniture/fixtures) carried at historical cost less depreciation/amortization.
- Provides useful lives: 1–4 years for computer equipment/software (including capitalized internal-use and website development), 3 years for furniture/fixtures, up to 30 years for buildings/improvements, and the shorter of 5 years or lease term for leasehold improvements.
- Describes capitalization of internal-use software and website development costs and their amortization within financial statement captions aligned with benefiting organizations; amounts capitalized were $511 million (2022) and $462 million (2021), with amortization expense of $426 million (2022), $366 million (2021), and $322 million (2020); maintenance costs are expensed.
- Outlines lease accounting: identification at inception; operating leases recognized as right-of-use (ROU) assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet.
- Covers sale-leaseback accounting, assessing transfer of control; if accounted for as financing, the asset remains on the balance sheet and proceeds are recorded as a financing obligation.
- Explains measurement of ROU assets and lease liabilities at commencement using present value of lease payments and an incremental borrowing rate; treatment of lease incentives and reasonably certain renewal/termination options; straight-line lease expense recognition.
- Describes impairment evaluation of ROU assets upon indicators or decisions to exit/sublease, assessed at the asset group or individual lease level, using undiscounted cash flows and measuring impairment at fair value when necessary.

nodes.title: Property and equipment
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.10 Property and equipment
nodes.start_phrase: Property and equipment consists primarily of computer equipment, software and website development costs, land and buildings, leasehold improvements, and furniture and fixtures.
nodes.summary:
- Part of PayPal’s Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements outlining significant accounting policies and related details.
- Funds receivable and payable: arise from clearing times in external payment networks for funding/withdrawals; typical clearing periods are 1–3 business days in the U.S. and up to 5 days internationally; includes amounts settled directly to customers’ bank accounts.
- Property and equipment: recorded at historical cost less accumulated depreciation/amortization; major asset classes include computer equipment, software and website development, land/buildings, leasehold improvements, and furniture/fixtures. Useful lives: 1–4 years for computer equipment and software (including capitalized internal-use software/website development), 3 years for furniture/fixtures, up to 30 years for buildings/improvements, and the shorter of 5 years or lease term for leasehold improvements.
- Internal-use software and website development: direct development costs capitalized and generally amortized over 3 years; $511 million capitalized in 2022 and $462 million in 2021; amortization expense was $426 million (2022), $366 million (2021), and $322 million (2020); maintenance costs expensed as incurred.
- Leases: identified at contract inception; operating leases recognized as right-of-use (ROU) assets (other assets) and lease liabilities (current and long-term). Sale-leasebacks evaluated for transfer of control; if not a sale, accounted for as financing (asset remains on balance sheet; proceeds as financing obligation).
- Lease measurement: ROU assets and liabilities recognized at commencement using the present value of lease payments; incremental borrowing rate used (no implicit rate); ROU includes lease payments and excludes incentives; includes extension/termination options when reasonably certain; straight-line lease expense over the lease term; remeasure upon decisions to renew/terminate.
- Impairment of ROU assets: assessed upon indicators/events (including exit/sublease decisions); evaluated at asset group or individual lease level; recoverability based on undiscounted cash flows; impairments measured at fair value using appropriate valuation techniques.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.11 Leases
nodes.start_phrase: We determine whether an arrangement is a lease for accounting purposes at contract inception.
nodes.summary:
- Explains “funds receivable and funds payable” as timing differences from clearing through external payment networks, typically 1–3 business days in the U.S. and up to 5 business days internationally, including amounts settled directly to customer bank accounts.
- Details property and equipment accounting: recorded at cost less accumulated depreciation; useful lives generally 1–4 years for computer equipment/software (including capitalized internal-use software and website development), 3 years for furniture and fixtures, up to 30 years for buildings/improvements, and the shorter of 5 years or lease term for leasehold improvements.
- Outlines capitalization of internal-use software/website development costs and amortization: capitalized $511 million (2022) and $462 million (2021); amortization expense of $426 million (2022), $366 million (2021), and $322 million (2020); maintenance costs expensed as incurred.
- Describes lease accounting under operating leases: recognition of right‑of‑use (ROU) assets and lease liabilities at commencement using the incremental borrowing rate; balance sheet presentation; straight-line lease expense; sale‑leaseback evaluation and potential financing method; treatment of renewal/termination options; ROU asset impairment assessment and measurement.
- Notes practical expedients and approaches: combining lease and non-lease components, expedients for classification, hindsight, and land easements; portfolio approach for ROU assets and liabilities.
- Covers goodwill and intangible assets: annual goodwill impairment testing at the reporting unit level (qualitative then quantitative if needed) using income (discounted cash flow) and market approaches; no impairment identified in tests as of August 31, 2022 and 2021, and no subsequent triggering events through December 31, 2022. Intangibles (customer lists/user base, marketing, developed technology, other) amortized straight-line over 2–7 years with no significant residual values.
- Provides impairment policy for long‑lived assets (including intangibles): assess recoverability upon indicators of impairment; assets impaired if carrying amount exceeds undiscounted future cash flows; measure impairment using fair value.
- Describes allowance for transaction losses: exposure to chargebacks, purchase protection claims, account takeovers, and seller nonperformance; allowance estimated from historical trends, case experience, mix of transactions/losses, and known facts; recorded in transaction and credit losses on the income statement and included in accrued expenses and other current liabilities on the balance sheet.

nodes.title: Goodwill and intangible assets
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.12 Goodwill and intangible assets
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill is tested for impairment, at a minimum, on an annual basis at the reporting unit level by first performing a qualitative assessment to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value of the reporting unit is less than its carrying value.
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting: Applies practical expedients to combine lease and non-lease components, and expedients for classification, hindsight, and land easements; uses a portfolio approach to recognize right-of-use assets and lease liabilities.
- Goodwill: Annual impairment testing at the reporting unit level starting with a qualitative assessment; if necessary, quantitative testing using income (discounted cash flow) and market approaches. No impairment identified in tests as of August 31, 2022 and 2021, and no subsequent triggering events through December 31, 2022.
- Intangible assets: Include customer lists/user base, marketing-related intangibles, developed technology, and other intangibles; amortized straight-line over 2–7 years with no significant residual values.
- Long-lived assets impairment: Reviewed when indicators arise; assets deemed impaired if carrying amount exceeds expected future undiscounted cash flows.
- Allowance for transaction losses: Recognizes expected losses from chargebacks, seller nonperformance, purchase protection claims, and account takeovers; allowance is data-driven, updated regularly, recorded in transaction and credit losses expense, and presented in accrued expenses and other current liabilities.

nodes.title: Impairment of long-lived assets
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.13 Impairment of long-lived assets
nodes.start_phrase: We evaluate long-lived assets (including intangible assets) for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of a long-lived asset may not be recoverable.
nodes.summary:
- Covers PayPal’s accounting policies and judgments related to leases, goodwill and intangible assets, impairment of long-lived assets, and allowance for transaction losses within the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Leases: PayPal applies practical expedients to treat lease and non-lease components as a single lease component, and uses expedients for lease classification, hindsight, and land easements. It accounts for right-of-use assets and lease liabilities using a portfolio approach.
- Goodwill: Tested for impairment annually at the reporting unit level using a qualitative screen followed by a fair value comparison if needed. Fair value may be determined using income (discounted cash flow) and market approaches. No goodwill impairment identified in the August 31, 2021 and 2022 tests; no subsequent triggering events through December 31, 2022.
- Intangible assets: Include customer lists/user base, marketing-related assets, developed technology, and other intangibles. Amortized on a straight-line basis over 2–7 years with no significant residual values.
- Impairment of long-lived assets: Evaluated when indicators arise; assets are impaired if carrying amounts exceed expected future undiscounted cash flows.
- Allowance for transaction losses: Recognizes exposure to fraud, chargebacks, seller nonperformance, purchase protection claims, and account takeovers. Establishes and regularly updates an allowance for probable losses (including those not yet identified) based on actual loss data, historical trends, and internal factors. Additions are recorded in transaction and credit losses on the income statement; the allowance is classified in accrued expenses and other current liabilities on the balance sheet.

nodes.title: Allowance for transaction losses
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.14 Allowance for transaction losses
nodes.start_phrase: We are exposed to transaction losses due to credit card and other payment misuse as well as nonperformance from sellers who accept payments through PayPal.
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting: Elected practical expedients to combine lease and non-lease components, apply classification, hindsight, and land easement expedients, and use a single portfolio approach for ROU assets and lease liabilities.
- Goodwill: Annual impairment testing at the reporting unit level using a qualitative screen followed by quantitative testing if needed; valuation via income (DCF) and market approaches. No goodwill impairment identified in 2021 or 2022; no triggering events through Dec 31, 2022 after the Aug 31, 2022 test.
- Intangible assets: Include customer lists/user base, marketing-related intangibles, developed technology, and other intangibles; amortized straight-line over 2–7 years with no significant residual values.
- Long-lived assets: Impairment testing when indicators arise; assets deemed impaired if carrying value exceeds expected undiscounted cash flows.
- Allowance for transaction losses: Covers credit card misuse, seller nonperformance, chargebacks, purchase protection claims, and account takeovers; based on historical loss data and qualitative factors; recorded in transaction and credit losses (P&L) and accrued expenses and other current liabilities (balance sheet).
- Allowance for negative customer balances: Arise from insufficient funds for ACH returns, debit transactions, and merchant chargebacks; recoverable via funding, incoming payments, backup sources, or collections. Loss estimate uses roll-rate modeling by delinquency bucket, qualitative adjustments as needed; write-offs at 120 days with recoveries reducing the allowance; presented in other current assets, net; P&L impact in transaction and credit losses.
- Derivative instruments: Additional details referenced in Note 10.
- Fair value measurement: Policies for recurring and non-recurring measurements; definition of fair value; use of observable inputs where possible; hierarchy levels 1–3 described; additional details in Note 9.
- Crypto asset safeguarding: Existence of safeguarding liability and corresponding asset; details in Note 7.

nodes.title: Allowance for negative customer balances
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.15 Allowance for negative customer balances
nodes.start_phrase: Negative customer balances occur primarily when there are insufficient funds in a customer’s PayPal account to cover charges applied for Automated Clearing House returns, debit card transactions, and merchant-related chargebacks due to non-delivery or unsatisfactory delivery of purchased items, which are generally within the scope of our protection programs.
nodes.summary:
- Explains PayPal’s policy for negative customer balances: causes (ACH returns, debit card transactions, chargebacks), methods of cure (customer funding, incoming payments, backup funding, third‑party collections), and the allowance methodology.
- Details allowance calculation for negative balances using historical loss data, roll rate models by delinquency bucket, consideration of qualitative adjustments, and write‑off policy at 120 days; recoveries reduce the allowance.
- States presentation: negative customer balances recorded in other current assets net of allowance; changes recorded in transaction and credit losses on the income statement.
- Describes fair value measurement framework: definition of fair value, use of observable vs. unobservable inputs, and the three‑level hierarchy (Levels 1–3); references Note 9 for more details.
- Notes existence of derivative instruments with a cross‑reference to Note 10.
- Mentions crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset, with a cross‑reference to Note 7.

nodes.title: Derivative instruments
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.16 Derivative instruments
nodes.start_phrase: See “Note 10—Derivative Instruments” for information related to the derivative instruments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains PayPal’s policy for negative customer balances: causes (ACH returns, debit card transactions, chargebacks), cure methods (funds added, incoming payments, backup funding, third‑party collections), and the allowance methodology. The allowance is based on historical collection/write‑off trends, internal factors, macroeconomic forecasts, and a roll‑rate model by delinquency bucket; balances are written off after 120 days, recoveries reduce the allowance, amounts are presented in other current assets net of allowance, and changes flow through transaction and credit losses.
- Describes the fair value measurement framework used for certain assets and liabilities on recurring and non‑recurring bases, emphasizing use of observable inputs and defining the Level 1–3 hierarchy.
- Cross‑references additional details: derivatives (Note 10), fair value measurements (Note 9), and crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset (Note 7).

nodes.title: Fair value measurements
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.17 Fair value measurements
nodes.start_phrase: We measure certain financial assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis and certain financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at fair value on a non-recurring basis when a change in fair value or impairment is evidenced.
nodes.summary:
- Explains PayPal’s policy for negative customer balances, including causes (ACH returns, debit card transactions, merchant chargebacks), cure methods (customer funding, incoming payments, backup funding, third-party collections), and the expected credit loss methodology. Losses are estimated using a roll rate model by delinquency bucket with historical trends, internal factors, and reasonable macroeconomic forecasts, followed by qualitative adjustments as needed. Negative balances are written off at 120 days; recoveries reduce the allowance. Balances are presented in other current assets, net of allowance, with adjustments recorded in transaction and credit losses.
- Outlines fair value measurement practices for recurring and non-recurring items, defining fair value, emphasizing use of observable inputs, and detailing the three-level hierarchy (Level 1, Level 2, Level 3). References Note 9 for additional details.
- References Note 10 for derivative instruments.
- References Note 7 for the crypto asset safeguarding liability and the corresponding safeguarding asset.

nodes.title: Crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.18 Crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset
nodes.start_phrase: See “Note 7—Other Financial Statement Details” for information related to our crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset.
nodes.summary:
- Continuation of PayPal Holdings, Inc. Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements outlining key accounting policies and risk disclosures.
- Allowance for negative customer balances: causes (ACH returns, debit transactions, chargebacks), cure methods, use of collection agencies; expected loss methodology using roll-rate models by delinquency bucket with historical trends, internal factors, and macroeconomic forecasts; quantitative/qualitative adjustments; write-off at 120 days; recoveries reduce the allowance; presentation in other current assets and expense in transaction and credit losses.
- Fair value measurements: definition of fair value; recurring vs. non-recurring measurement; hierarchy levels (Level 1, 2, 3) with inputs explained; reference to Note 9 for details.
- Derivative instruments: referenced to Note 10 for further information.
- Crypto asset safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset: referenced to Note 7.
- Concentrations of risk: potential credit risk across cash, equivalents, investments, receivables, loans, funds receivable and customer accounts, and notes receivable; deposits and investments held with high-quality institutions, balances exceed FDIC limits with ongoing credit monitoring; AR and lending exposure across U.S. and international customers; one customer accounted for 20% (2022) and 25% (2021) of net AR; no customer >10% of net loans receivable; one partner institution comprised long-term notes receivable equal to 18% (2022) and 22% (2021) of other assets; revenue concentration—no customer >10% of net revenues; eBay Marketplaces represented ~2% (2022), 6% (2021), 13% (2020); no other source >10%.
- Revenue recognition: referenced to Note 2.
- Advertising expense: recognition policies (production at incurrence; media on use; online based on impressions, pay-per-click, or straight-line); expenses of $518M (2022), $740M (2021), $654M (2020).
- Defined contribution savings plans: U.S. 401(k) and non-U.S. plans; expenses recognized as services are rendered.
- Stock-based compensation: RSUs/PSUs/RSAs measured at grant-date stock price; options valued via Black-Scholes; straight-line expense over vesting for awards expected to vest; expense reduced for estimated forfeitures based on termination behavior and historical trends.

nodes.title: Concentrations of risk
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.19 Concentrations of risk
nodes.start_phrase: Our cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, accounts receivable, loans and interest receivable, net, funds receivable and customer accounts, long-term investments, and long-term notes receivable, are potentially subject to concentration of credit risk.
nodes.summary:
- Concentrations of risk: Discussion of credit and counterparty risk across cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, accounts receivable, loans and interest receivable, funds receivable and customer accounts, long-term investments, and long-term notes receivable. Cash and funds are held with high-credit-quality institutions; investments are highly liquid and uninsured; corporate deposits exceed FDIC limits with periodic counterparty credit reviews. Receivables and loans arise from U.S. and international customers; long-term note relates to deferred proceeds from a 2018 sale of U.S. consumer credit receivables.
- Concentration metrics: One customer represented 20% (2022) and 25% (2021) of net accounts receivable; no customer >10% of net loans receivable (2022, 2021). One partner institution comprised the entire long-term notes receivable, equaling 18% (2022) and 22% (2021) of other assets. No customer accounted for >10% of net revenues in 2020–2022. Revenue from eBay’s Marketplaces platform was approximately 2% (2022), 6% (2021), and 13% (2020); no other source exceeded 10%.
- Revenue recognition: Refers to Note 2 for detailed revenue recognition policies.
- Advertising expense: Production costs expensed when incurred; media costs expensed when run. Online ads recognized by impressions delivered, pay-per-click, or straight-line over contract term. Advertising expense totaled $518 million (2022), $740 million (2021), and $654 million (2020).
- Defined contribution savings plans: U.S. 401(k) and non-U.S. plans; expenses recognized as employee services are rendered.
- Stock-based compensation: RSUs, performance RSUs, and restricted stock measured at grant-date fair value of common stock; stock options valued using Black-Scholes. Expense recognized on a straight-line basis over vesting for awards expected to vest, reduced for estimated forfeitures based on observed employee termination and forfeiture trends.

nodes.title: Revenue recognition
nodes.heading: 15.7.2.20 Revenue recognition
nodes.start_phrase: See “Note 2—Revenue” for information related to our revenue recognition.
nodes.summary:
- Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (PayPal Holdings, Inc.) covering risk concentrations, expense policies, and compensation accounting.
- Concentrations of risk: Various financial assets (cash, investments, receivables, loans, funds receivable, notes) subject to credit risk; funds held with high-credit-quality institutions; investments are highly liquid and rated but uninsured; corporate deposits exceed FDIC limits with ongoing credit monitoring. Receivables and loans arise from U.S. and international customers. nodes.title: TRANSACTION REVENUES

nodes.summary:
- Recently adopted accounting guidance: PayPal adopted SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 121 (SAB 121) in Q2 2022 with retrospective application to January 1, 2022. SAB 121 requires recognition of a safeguarding liability and corresponding safeguarding asset, measured at the fair value of customers’ crypto assets, along with related disclosures. As of June 30, 2022, PayPal recorded $596 million for both the liability (accrued expenses and other current liabilities) and the asset (prepaid expenses and other current assets). Other new accounting pronouncements are not expected to be material.

- Revenue (Note 2) overview: PayPal earns revenue primarily from processing payments and from other value added services, classified into:
  - Transaction revenues
  - Revenues from other value added services

- Transaction revenues:
  - Earned from fees to receive payments, comprising fixed and variable components; variable fees are known at processing and may be partially refundable. Estimated fee refunds reduce revenue.
  - Additional fees arise from currency conversion, cross-border transactions, instant transfers, crypto purchase/sale facilitation, contractual compensation from sellers violating terms, and miscellaneous items; incentives reduce revenue.
  - Contracts are open-ended, defined at the transaction level, auto-renewing, and cancellable without penalty; tiered pricing does not create a material right; no capitalized contract costs or material contract balances.
  - Single performance obligation: complete payment transactions. Revenue is recognized on a gross basis as principal due to control over the service, primary responsibility, pricing discretion, and margin risk. Processor/banking fees are recorded as transaction expense; PayPal provides customer support.
  - Merchant/consumer protection programs are not separate services; related costs are recognized in transaction and credit losses when transactions occur.
  - Incentives: amounts deemed consideration payable to customers (or paid on their behalf) reduce revenue; other incentives to non-customers are sales and marketing expense.

- Revenues from other value added services:
  - Include partnerships, referral fees, subscriptions, gateway fees, and other merchant/consumer services.
  - Typically involve one performance obligation recognized over the contract term; prices are generally fixed, with some estimated via expected value method.
  - Recorded on a net basis when PayPal acts as an agent.
  - Interest and fee income from loans receivable and interest on certain assets underlying customer balances are recognized using the effective interest method, net of reserves and deferred cost amortization.

- Disaggregation and segments:
  - PayPal operates as one operating and reportable segment; the CEO is the CODM reviewing consolidated results.
  - Revenue is disaggregated by primary geographic markets and by type (transaction revenues and revenues from other value added services), reflecting similar products, fees, and recognition models within each category.

- Notes interest and fee income from loans receivable and interest on assets underlying customer balances, recognized using the effective interest method and presented net of reserves and deferred cost amortization.
- States the company operates as a single reportable segment; the CEO is the CODM reviewing consolidated results; revenue is disaggregated by primary geographic markets and by revenue type (transaction revenues and other value added services) reflecting similar products, fee structures, and recognition models within categories.

- Explains accounting for incentives to merchants and consumers (discounts, rebates, rewards, coupons): judged to determine if they are consideration payable to a customer; such amounts reduce revenue; incentives to non-customers are recorded in sales and marketing expense.

- Outlines revenues from other value-added services (partnerships, referral fees, subscriptions, gateway fees, and other services): typically a single performance obligation recognized over the contract term; transaction price generally fixed, sometimes estimated via expected value; recognized on a net basis when PayPal acts as agent.

- Recurring fair value measurements: Detailed tables as of December 31, 2022 and 2021 for assets and liabilities by Level 1 and Level 2, covering:

- Fair value option election: PayPal elects the fair value option for available-for-sale debt securities denominated in non-functional currencies to reduce earnings volatility from FX-related accounting asymmetry; related gains/losses are recorded in other income (expense), net. Balances under this option declined significantly from 2021 to 2022, with associated net losses recognized in both years.
- Non-recurring fair value measurements: 
  - Non-marketable equity securities under the Measurement Alternative were remeasured based on observable price changes (Level 2) or impairment (Level 3). 2022 included both Level 2 and Level 3 amounts; 2021 amounts were Level 2 only. Significant portions each year were not remeasured due to no observable price changes.
  - Other assets consist of ROU lease assets written down due to impairment, measured using observable market data and classified as Level 2.
- Measurement methodologies:
  - Non-marketable equity securities measured at cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes; Level 2 when remeasured on observable transactions; Level 3 when impaired using unobservable inputs (e.g., discount rates, forecast cash flows, market comps).
  - ROU lease asset impairments estimated using market-derived rental metrics and classified as Level 2.
- Financial instruments not carried at fair value: Many instruments (cash, restricted cash, time deposits, certain customer accounts, loans/interest receivable, and credit facility borrowings) are at amortized cost approximating fair value. Disclosures provide carrying vs. fair values for notes receivable and fixed-rate notes for 2022 and 2021. If measured at fair value, classification would be: cash Level 1; restricted cash, time deposits, certain customer accounts, and long-term debt Level 2; remaining instruments Level 3.
- Derivative instruments: Used primarily to hedge foreign currency exchange risk, not for trading or speculation. Counterparty credit risk is managed via limiting to major institutions, diversification, collateral arrangements, and ongoing monitoring.

nodes.title: SUMMARY OF DERIVATIVE INSTRUMENTS
nodes.heading: 15.16.1 SUMMARY OF DERIVATIVE INSTRUMENTS
nodes.start_phrase: Our primary objective in holding derivatives is to reduce the volatility of earnings and cash flows associated with changes in foreign currency exchange rates.
nodes.summary:
- Describes fair value measurement for non-marketable equity securities under the Measurement Alternative: carried at cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes; Level 2 classification when remeasured using observable transaction prices; Level 3 when impaired using unobservable inputs (e.g., discount rates, forecasted cash flows, comparable market data).
- Discusses impairment evaluation of right-of-use (ROU) assets for leases; impairments for office operating leases use market-derived rental rates and are classified as Level 2.
- Outlines financial assets and liabilities carried at amortized cost (cash, restricted cash, time deposits, loans and interest receivable, certain customer accounts, and credit-facility debt) and provides fair value disclosures:
  - Notes receivable: $441m carrying vs. $396m fair value (Dec 31, 2022); $381m carrying vs. $424m fair value (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Fixed-rate notes: $10.3b carrying vs. $9.5b fair value (Dec 31, 2022); $9.0b carrying vs. $9.3b fair value (Dec 31, 2021).
  - If measured at fair value: cash Level 1; restricted cash, time deposits, certain customer accounts, and long-term debt Level 2; remaining instruments Level 3.
- Summarizes derivative instruments policy: used to reduce foreign currency exchange risk; counterparty credit risk managed via major institutions, diversification, and collateral; no trading/speculative use.
- Cash flow hedges: FX contracts (generally ≤18 months) hedge forecasted foreign-currency revenues; gains/losses recorded in AOCI and reclassified to revenue when hedged transactions occur; effectiveness assessed via critical-terms match; operating cash flow classification; $110m of net gains in AOCI expected to be reclassified to earnings within 12 months as of Dec 31, 2022; no discontinued cash flow hedges in 2020–2022.
- Net investment hedges: forward FX contracts hedge investments in foreign subsidiaries; effective portion recorded in AOCI (foreign currency translation); forward points recognized in other income (expense) over the hedge life; cash flows classified as investing; no AOCI reclassifications to earnings in the periods presented.
- Non-designated FX contracts: used to offset FX risk on monetary assets/liabilities; remeasurement gains/losses recorded in other income (expense) and offset by derivative results; operating cash flow classification.

nodes.title: Cash flow hedges
nodes.heading: 15.16.2 Cash flow hedges
nodes.start_phrase: We have significant international revenues and costs denominated in foreign currencies, which subjects us to foreign currency exchange risk.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt outlines PayPal’s use of foreign currency risk management through derivatives, covering cash flow hedges, net investment hedges, and non-designated foreign currency contracts.
- Cash flow hedges: PayPal designates short-dated (generally ≤18 months) FX contracts to hedge forecasted foreign-currency revenues, aiming to reduce USD cash flow volatility. Gains/losses are initially recorded in AOCI and reclassified to revenue when the hedged transactions affect earnings. Hedge effectiveness is assessed quarterly via critical-terms matching with no components excluded. Related cash flows are classified as operating activities. As of Dec 31, 2022, $110 million of net gains in AOCI are expected to be reclassified to earnings within 12 months. No cash flow hedges were discontinued in 2020–2022 due to non-occurrence of forecasted transactions.
- Discontinuation policy: If a cash flow hedge is discontinued but the forecasted transaction is still probable, gains/losses remain in AOCI until the transaction affects earnings; otherwise, gains/losses after discontinuation or for non-designated instruments are recorded in the related financial statement line item.
- Net investment hedges: PayPal uses forward FX contracts to hedge investments in certain foreign subsidiaries. The effective portion of gains/losses is recorded in AOCI within foreign currency translation and remains there until the subsidiaries are sold or substantially liquidated, at which point amounts are reclassified to earnings. Forward points are excluded from effectiveness assessment and recognized in other income (expense), net on a straight-line basis. Related cash flows are classified as investing activities. No reclassifications from AOCI to earnings occurred in the periods presented.
- Non-designated FX contracts: Used to offset FX risk on monetary assets and liabilities denominated in non-functional currencies. Remeasurement gains/losses on these items are recorded in other income (expense), net and are offset by gains/losses on the related FX contracts. Cash flows are classified as operating activities.

nodes.title: Net investment hedges
nodes.heading: 15.16.3 Net investment hedges
nodes.start_phrase: We use forward foreign currency exchange contracts to reduce the foreign currency exchange risk related to our investment in certain foreign subsidiaries.
nodes.summary:
- The note describes PayPal’s foreign currency risk management and accounting for derivatives across three categories: cash flow hedges, net investment hedges, and non-designated foreign currency exchange contracts.
- Cash flow hedges:
  - Use of short-dated (generally ≤18 months) foreign currency exchange contracts to mitigate volatility in forecasted foreign-currency revenues.
  - Designated as cash flow hedges; gains/losses initially recorded in AOCI and reclassified into revenue when the hedged transactions impact earnings.
  - Hedge effectiveness assessed quarterly by matching critical terms; no components excluded from effectiveness testing.
  - Cash flows from these derivatives classified as operating activities.
  - As of December 31, 2022, approximately $110 million of net derivative gains in AOCI expected to be reclassified into earnings within 12 months.
  - No cash flow hedges were discontinued in 2020–2022; policy for discontinuation outlined (retain in AOCI if the forecasted transaction remains probable; otherwise reclassify).
  - Gains/losses on derivatives after discontinuation and on non-designated instruments recorded in the related financial statement line item.
- Net investment hedges:
  - Use of forward FX contracts to hedge investments in certain foreign subsidiaries.
